text: You've written stored procedures that run a batch of statements. A scalar user-defined function is different — it's a single value, computed from its parameters, that you call the same way you'd call a built-in function like LEN or GETDATE.

Create function dbo dot ProductMargin, taking a list price and a standard cost, returns money. The body is a BEGIN/END block, just like you've already seen, except instead of running statements for their side effects, it ends with RETURN and a single value — here, list price minus standard cost.

Once it exists, you call it exactly like any built-in expression — dbo dot ProductMargin, list price, standard cost, right inside the SELECT list. It reads beautifully. Every query that needs a margin can just call the function instead of repeating the subtraction everywhere.

Here's what that readability can cost you. SQL Server's optimizer treats a scalar function as a black box. Instead of folding your logic into its normal set-based plan, it calls the function once per row. On a few rows, invisible. On a large table, that can block parallelism, degrade the optimizer's row estimates, and quietly turn a fast query into a slow one — for reasons that don't show up just by reading the query.

SQL Server 2019 changed part of this story. At compatibility level 150 or higher, the optimizer can automatically rewrite a simple scalar function into an equivalent set-based expression and fold it into the plan — scalar UDF inlining. But it only applies to functions simple enough to translate safely. TRY/CATCH, non-deterministic calls, and manual error handling still disqualify a function, so the old caveat is narrower now, not gone.
Next lesson looks at a different kind of function — one the optimizer never has to treat as a black box in the first place: the inline table-valued function.
